newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Rebel Tajik commander agrees to withdraw troops.
newsitem.headline: Rebel Tajik commander agrees to withdraw troops.

text.p: The mutinous commander of Tajikistan's elite armoured brigade promised on Thursday to obey his president and return to barracks.
But his decision to send in tanks and armour against the irregular force of a local opponent highlighted the remote, Central Asian republic's slide into armed anarchy.
Brigade commander Makhmud Khudoyberdyev told reporters in the western town of Shakhrinau that most of his unit would return to its base near the southern town of Kurgan-Tyube on Thursday.
"We will be leaving in half an hour," he said, adding that a small "mobile group" would remain to "restore order".

Sporting the three stars of a colonel on crisp combat dress, Khudoyberdyev also spoke to reporters in a squat official building in nearby Tursunzade, an aluminium smelting town 45 km (30 miles) west of the capital Dushanbe.

"I do not think there are any disagreements,' he told journalists, of his relations with embattled Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov. "Because I think the president needs a strong arm," he added, allowing himself an ironic smile.

On Wednesday, Rakhmonov threatened to treat his renegade commander as a "war criminal" after Khudoyberdyev moved troops and armour on his own initiative to Tursunzade to rid the town of local strongman Kodir Abdulayev.
"When a man kills people, women, you have to ask who is the criminal," said Khudoyberdyev. "Commander Khudoyberdyev or the criminal Abdulayev."

The colonel said Abdulayev had "run off into the hills like an antelope". Parked below his window were five tanks and assorted armour. Around them lolled 200 or so tired but confident troops nursing Kalashnikov assault rifles.
After the fighting the previous day, children were back on the streets of Tursunzade, tearing around indulgent mothers in glittering traditional shirts and leggings.
Khudoyberdyev's run-in with the president is not the first.
In February last year, the colonel led a revolt, demanding the removal of 'corrupt' officials. Rakhmonov backed down.
The Tajik leader has his hands full already, trying to suppress a four-year Islamic insurgency in the former Soviet republic, which has left tens of thousands dead.
A preliminary peace accord was signed with the Islamist opposition in Moscow last month and talks on power-sharing were held in the Iranian capital Tehran this week.
But diplomats say Rakhmonov's shaky administration is threatened more by the mushrooming armed bands intent on carving up the republic's cotton, metals and drugs trade.
"It's not so much a question of government or opposition troops anymore," said a seasoned Western diplomat in Dushanbe.
"Armed groups are sprouting up all over the place."
In Shakhrinau, situated between Tursunzade and Dushanbe, unidentified armed men in civilian dress were stopping vehicles.
Islamist guerrillas control the eastern half of the mountain nation, where 10 percent of the 5.7 million population lives.
Rakhmonov's grip even on the capital is tenuous. Russian army peacekeepers based in the city have been the victims of Algerian-style shootings and bombings.
With his own troops occasionally out of control, Rakhmonov is having problems halting the republic's slide into the same armed anarchy which has bedevilled neighbouring Afghanistan.
Underlying the war are bitter clan and regional rivalries.

"It is very difficult for us here," said 73-year-old Akhmed, a retired factory worker in Tursunzade. As he spoke, a gang of youths armed with Kalashnikov rifles half-heartedly tried to requisition a man's car. "With all this fighting, it is difficult to see how there will be peace,' Akhmed said.
